extracted.intended_audience: educators, librarians, parents, and others selecting inclusive children's literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for educators/librarians/parents on critically selecting children's books that represent disability experiences, focusing on characterization, narrative voice, reader positioning, relationships, and demographic diversity. Offers concrete questions and examples of anti-patterns to identify humanizing versus dehumanizing texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character multidimensionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author/illustrator present the character with a disability label as multidimensional?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disability label is one identity marker—often not one a character has chosen. Memorable main characters are multidimensional and complex. Additional layers of identity should be presented over the course of the story through decisions, situations, and relationships. Anti-pattern: characters who do not develop or who are reduced to a label, leaving the reader with little information other than that label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative ownership / who gets to tell the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Whose story is this and who gets to tell it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid texts where disability is narrated primarily from the perspective of a sibling or friend who speaks for the person with a label. Prefer humanizing texts written from a first-person perspective that center the voice of the character with a label. Third-person narration can work only when it offers access to the character's own thoughts and perspective rather than speaking for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader positioning and portrayal (avoid pity/dehumanization)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reader, how have you been positioned to think about/feel about the character with a disability label in this book?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for representations that position characters as objects of pity who need care and do not show their contributions to community (e.g., 'class pet' dynamics). Humanizing literature may depict marginalization but does so in complex ways that acknowledge exclusion while also showing character agency, perseverance, and contribution. Anti-patterns: pity narratives, dehumanizing portrayals, one-note suffering without agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic, reciprocal relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: What opportunities does the character with a disability label have in the book to engage in authentic relationships?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality texts show relationships in which both parties contribute to the relationship rather than one-sided support. Avoid one-dimensional friendships where the character with a label exists only to be cared for or supervised. Strong books may portray complicated relationships (exclusion, bullying, adversity) but also model realistic, reciprocal friendships and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid universalizing disability; acknowledge histories of exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the text treat disability as a single, universal experience or acknowledge multiple, contextual meanings and histories?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disability labels carry histories of exclusion and are often used without unpacking their meanings, which can suggest there is only one experience of disability. Good selections avoid universalizing or flattening disability and instead reflect varied experiences and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: representation over didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the book primarily designed to teach 'what a disability is' or to provide representation and mirrors/windows for readers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusive children’s literature is not necessarily designed to teach children about what a disability is. Instead, it should provide opportunities for those with disability labels to see experiences like theirs and for typically developing students to see difference without making the text solely didactic. Books should center lived experience rather than functioning as a how-to lesson about disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersectional and demographic diversity (avoid narrow casting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the book reflect diversity across race, gender, class, and other identity markers among characters with disabilities, or does it reproduce narrow patterns?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of over-representation of white male characters (e.g., prosthetic users) and the repetition of narrow tropes. Quality collections include characters of varied racial, gender, socioeconomic, and cultural backgrounds, showing that disability intersects with other identities rather than appearing as a single-axis experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection resources and review sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Where to look for high-quality humanizing inclusive titles and reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established awards and own-voices review sources as starting points: e.g., the Schneider Family Book Award (ALA) for winners in young readers/middle grade/teen categories; blogs and review sites by disabled reviewers such as Disability in KidLit, the Indigo Project, and the Disability Visibility Project. These resources help identify titles reviewed or created by those who identify as disabled.
